title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the offer to the message you send

questions.prompt: The five sentences of this e-mail have been shuffled. No greeting and no signature are left to guide you: only the words that point backwards do. Put the sentences back in the order the writer sent them.

options.text: Neither of these two promises carries a price, however, and a price is what my group needs first.
I read your advertisement for the Spring Oasis Pass in the March issue of Travel Weekly.
Finally, I'd like to know more about the craft exhibition, since we shall have only one free afternoon.
It promises free admission to the four official sites and a discount at the craft market.
There are twenty-four of us, so could you tell me what that would come to per person?

questions.explanation: The order is not a template you learn by heart: each sentence names something in the sentence before it, and that is what fixes the chain. "It" can only be the advertisement, so the line that mentions the advertisement has to open the message. "These two promises" can only be the free admission and the discount, so it comes after the line that makes them. "That" in the question about the cost per person can only be the price just declared missing. And "finally" closes. Take those small words away and the same five sentences collapse into a list the reader has to reassemble himself — which is exactly what they are there to prevent, in an e-mail as in a paragraph.

questions.prompt: The stress in "announced" falls on its second syllable: a-NOUNCED. Which line describes the letter a of the opening syllable correctly?

options.text: the [æ] of "package", since the letter written is an a
the [ɑː] of "chance" as the British say it
the weak [ə], because the syllable carries no stress
the [eɪ] of "name", because the syllable is open

questions.explanation: The weak [ə] lives only where the stress does not, and the opening syllable here carries none: the voice hurries over it to reach a-NOUNCED. Its vowel loses all its colour and becomes the commonest sound in English, the one heard at the beginning of "about" and again at the end of "teacher". The letter on the page decides nothing at all — the same a is the wide-open [æ] in package, where it is stressed, and [ə] here, where it is not. Find the stress first and the vowel follows on its own.

questions.prompt: A brochure says the pass opens "several official sites". A pupil writes in his notebook: "the pass opens 2 sites". Why is his note wrong?

options.text: several means more than two, but not very many
several means at least ten of the sites that are listed
several means every one of them, without exception
several is another way of writing the number two

questions.explanation: Several is a quantity word and not a figure: it says more than two, and not very many — three, four, five, somewhere in that country. Two is precisely what it rules out, so a note that turns it into 2 has invented a fact the brochure never printed. Ten would already be many, and every one of them is what "all" or "the whole of" would have said. This is why several is useless in the column of a table: it cannot be counted, and a reader who counts it has stopped reading the advertisement and started writing it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence can a pupil send in his e-mail to the festival office exactly as it stands?

options.text: I am very interesting in your festival programme.
Your festival programme is very interested.
I am very interesting about your festival programme.
I am very interested in your festival programme.

questions.explanation: The two endings share out the roles: -ed goes to the person who feels something, -ing to the thing that causes the feeling. A reader is interested and a programme is interesting, never the other way round — a pupil who writes that he is interesting is announcing that he is what the visitors have come to look at, and a programme that is interested would be one taking notes on him. The preposition is fixed as well: you are interested in something, never about it. Two small letters and one preposition, and the message either does its work or comes back.

questions.prompt: Step 2 of your project asks you to describe a festival you know well to the people who will read your page on the Web. Which opening does what Step 2 asks?

options.text: For three days in April, a whole town on the coast puts its sky to work.
The Kite Festival takes place every April in a town on the northern coast.
The Kite Festival is a wonderful festival that nobody should miss.
I like the Kite Festival very much and I go back to it every year.

questions.explanation: A web page has to make a stranger want to come, and the way to do it is to show the one thing that belongs to this festival and to no other — a town that spends three days filling its own sky. Dates and places are facts your reader needs, and they will go on the page, but on their own they describe a hundred festivals equally well. Calling a festival wonderful and unmissable persuades nobody, since anyone can write that sentence about anything. And your own pleasure in going back every year is about you, not about the festival. Describing attractively is persuading with the truth: you invent nothing, you choose what to show.

questions.prompt: A festival page prints: "Come and join us — three days you will remember, and a welcome you will not find anywhere else." A pupil says the page tells him what the festival offers. What is wrong with what he says?

options.text: The page gives the dates but never mentions the price of a ticket.
The page praises the festival without naming one thing you can do there.
The page names the events but never says who is allowed to take part in them.
The page is written to inform the reader rather than to attract him.

questions.explanation: Read the line again and count the facts in it: there are none. Three days you will remember, and a welcome like no other, are promises, and nothing in either can be checked, booked or paid for. The page prints no dates, so it cannot be blamed for giving them without a price; it names no event, so nobody can be excluded from one; and it is plainly written to attract rather than to inform, which is what an advertisement is for. The mistake is to take praise for information. When a page tells you only how good it is going to be, that is the moment the pen comes out and the questions get written down.
